There is a house on my street that no one has ever seen anyone move into.

It's the blue one on the corner, with the porch that sags a little in the middle. The paint is not quite peeling, but thinking about it. Every morning on my walk, I pass it and I look at the curtains — white, sheer, always closed — and I think: someone must have chosen those. Someone measured that window. Someone stood on that porch with a key for the first time.

I have lived on this street for seven years and I have never seen them.

For a while I invented stories. A widow who only goes out at night. A writer who has groceries delivered and works by lamplight. A man who is hiding from something, and does a very good job of it. Then for a while I forgot about it completely, because that's what happens to mysteries that don't ask anything of you. They fade into the architecture of your life.

Until last Tuesday.

Last Tuesday it rained. Not a storm, just that thin, discourteous drizzle that makes everyone walk a little faster and look a little more alone. I was coming back from the store with a bag of clementines and a loaf of bread that was getting damp through the paper, and I saw that the front door of the blue house was open. Just an inch. Just enough to see a bar of yellow light inside.

I stopped. I don't know why. There was no reason to stop. But there is a very specific feeling you get when a thing that has always been closed is suddenly open, even a little. It's not curiosity, exactly. It's more like vertigo. As if the world has skipped a track.

A woman was standing on the porch.

She wasn't what I expected. I had imagined someone pale and hermit-like, but she was in a bright yellow raincoat that was far too big for her, and she was holding a chipped mug. She saw me looking and smiled, and it was such a normal, unmysterious smile that I laughed out of relief.

“You’re staring at my house,” she said.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “I’ve just never seen anyone here. I live down there. Number 14.”

“I know,” she said. “You walk your dog at 7:15. You listen to podcasts too loud. You always double back because you forget your keys.”

I felt my face go hot. She said it kindly, though. As if reciting a favorite poem.

“I’m Mara,” she said. “You want to come in for a second? Out of the rain.”

That should have been strange. I did not know this woman. But there are times in life when saying yes is easier than figuring out why you should say no. The rain was picking up, dotting the top of my bread bag. So I followed her in.

The inside of the house was not what I expected either. From the street, I had imagined it dark, cluttered, airless. It was the opposite. It was almost entirely empty. The floors were bare wood, polished. The walls were white. There was one chair in the living room. One table. And everywhere, on every surface, were jars.

Hundreds of them. Maybe a thousand. Mason jars, jam jars, old pickle jars, tiny apothecary vials. All empty? No — not empty. Each one held something that caught the light differently.

“What is this?” I asked.

“My collection,” she said. She picked up a jar from the table nearest the door. Inside it, there was nothing I could see, and then, when she tilted it, a flicker. Like dust in a sunbeam. “This one is from last Thursday. About 4 p.m. The sun came out after raining all day and everyone on the street stopped at the same time to look up. Remember? It lasted about eight seconds.”

I stared at her.

“This one,” she said, picking up another, “is from three years ago. A kid learned to ride a bike right out there on the sidewalk. He fell seven times. On the eighth, his father let go and didn't tell him. He rode for twelve feet before he realized no one was holding him. He screamed.”

She laughed. “Joy, mostly. A little terror.”

I thought she was doing a bit. A very committed art piece. I smiled politely and set my groceries down.

“You collect… moments?” I said, trying to sound game.

“Seconds,” she said. “Just seconds. People don't think seconds are anything. They think minutes are the smallest thing that counts. But seconds are where your life actually happens.”

She unscrewed a jar. I felt a puff of air, cool against my face, smelling faintly of cut grass and sunscreen. And for a half second I wasn't in that empty house at all. I was nine, in my parents' backyard, and my mother had just turned on the sprinkler and I was running through it in my clothes, shrieking, and she was laughing so hard she had to sit down in the wet grass.

Then it was gone. I was back, holding my damp bread, blinking.

“How did you do that?” I whispered.

Mara screwed the lid back on, gently. “You don't keep a moment by remembering it hard. You keep it by letting it go at the right time.”

She walked through the house, and I followed. She showed me jars that contained the second a woman at the grocery store decided not to buy the cheap eggs but the expensive free-range ones, because this once she wanted to feel luxurious. A second where two strangers on a bus made eye contact and both looked away smiling for no reason. The second my neighbor, Mr. Albescu, who never talks to anyone, found a ladybug on his sleeve and spoke to it very softly in Romanian.

“They're all here,” she said. “All the little ones that would have disappeared.”

“Why?” I said. My voice was very small.

“Because someone has to notice,” she said. “Otherwise what's the point? The big things remember themselves. Weddings, funerals, graduations — they hire photographers. No one photographs the way light looks on the kitchen floor at 3:47 on a random February afternoon. But that might be the second you finally felt at home again after being lonely for months.”

She stopped at a jar on the windowsill. It was empty.

“This one,” she said, “is for right now.”

I looked at her. The rain ticked against the windows. The house smelled like old wood and rain and faintly, impossibly, of clementines.

“What happens in this one?” I asked.

She smiled. “You tell me.”

And I stood there, and I realized I had been holding my breath. I don't know for how long. Maybe for years in some small, measurable way. I breathed out. The groceries crinkled. Outside, a car passed, spraying water.

It was just a second. One thin, drizzly Tuesday second in a blue house that I had walked past a thousand times without ever really seeing.

Mara lifted the lid.

I left a few minutes later. She didn't ask for my name again. She already knew it. At the door she pressed something into my hand — not a jar, just a smooth, ordinary river stone, warm from where she'd held it.

“You'll know when to use it,” she said.

I walked home in the rain. My dog barked when I came in, annoyed I'd been gone so long without him. I put the clementines in a bowl. I put the stone on my windowsill.

I haven't seen the blue house open since. The curtains are still white. The porch still sags. But now, every night at 7:15 when I walk the dog, I don't listen to my podcast. I leave my earbuds at home. I listen to the seconds ticking by, one after another, like jars lining a shelf that never ends.

And sometimes, just sometimes, I catch one.
